newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Investors praise Hungary, worry over opposition.
newsitem.headline: Investors praise Hungary, worry over opposition.

text.p: Foreign investors welcomed Hungarian Prime Minister Gyula Horn's message that stability is assured no matter who wins next year's elections but expressed worries about recent opposition party statements.

"One of our concerns is some attitudes of Hungary's opposition," said Ivan Volgyes, director for Hungary at General Electric Co of the U.S. "We feel that we are being singled out in political speeches," he told a conference of international investors in Budapest on Tuesday.

Hungarian opposition party the Democratic Forum said last week it would initiate a referendum against a government plan to allow the indirect purchase of farmland by foreigners through companies, adding that all five opposition parties were against the land plan.

The leader of the largest opposition party, Jozsef Torgyan has repeatedly opposed the sale of Hungarian state assets and has said his party, the Independent Smallholders, would re-examine all privatisation contracts if it came to power.
Volgyes said he was concerned particularly about opposition criticism of multinationals.

"The multinationals are the story behind Hungary's economic success," he said, adding that Hungary's privatisation programme in which it has put 75 percent of its economy into private hands was "the greatest success in history."

GE, Hungary's biggest foreign investor, acquired 50 percent of the Tungsram lighting company in 1989 and now wholly owns the company. In 1995 its financing arm GE Capital Services acquired a 27.4 percent stake with management rights of Budapest Bank, with registered capital of 20 billion forints.

Horn, speaking earlier at what was billed as a summit conference for investors, told an audience of more than 100 businessmen, diplomats and officials that Hungary no longer needed drastic economic restructuring measures.

He said a shock austerity programme already in place had stabilised the economy, bringing inflation down from more than 30 percent to an anticipated 13 to 13.5 percent year on year next year, and had prompted a resumption of economic growth.

"We are close to the average of the lower-income member states of the European Union," said Horn, whose Socialist Party and allied Free Democrats have a majority in Parliament ahead of May 1998 elections.

"No matter what the outcome of the elections, there should be continuity that has characterised Hungarian economic growth so far," Horn told the audience in a banquet hall of one of Budapest's luxury restaurants.

Judit Csiha, Hungary's privatisation minister and head of the APV Rt privatisation agency, said Hungary had succeeded in privatisation by quickly selling strategic sectors such as banks and telecommunications.
"More or less we can state that the privatisation process has fulfilled its responsibility. We have come to the end of this process," Csiha said.
Another important foreign investor, Sony, said its decision last year to centre its manufacturing for the region in Hungary had been the correct one.

"Hungary was most suitable (in Central Europe) because of its rapid progress in globalisation, its high quality but inexpensive labour force and its relatively developed infrastructure," Sony Hungary's managing director Shugi Minemura told the conference.
"Although some differences remain in business style we can call our investment a success."

Sony began production at its new $20 million assembly plant at Godollo, east of Budapest, in January. The plant currently produces CD players from parts imported from Singapore, Western Europe and Japan and will later manufacture mini stereo systems, colour TVs and video cassette recorders.
